So Virginia Freedom of Information Act is state law governing access of all citizens in Virginia to public records. It also requires that all public meetings be open and that all records are presumed to be open, with the caveat that there are exemptions to that. So what is a public record? A lot of times we get a lot of questions about that.

It's anything that's in writing, in any format, video, audio, notes. A Post-it could be considered a public record, so long as it is something that is done and the content is related to the public entity, in this case, school or scholastic-related information. So what's a FOIA request? This is any request for public records.

This can come in any format. It can be a passing comment. It can be a formal submission into our GovQA platform. It could be an email. It can be a phone call. Any request for public records is automatically deemed a FOIA request. They do not need to say the magic words, "This is a Freedom of Information Act request." So the general rule is that public records must be disclosed upon request.

Now, there are some stipulations that I'll get into in a minute. So who has the right? All residents of the Commonwealth. Whenever someone submits a request into GovQA, that's going to be one of the questions is verifying the identity. A lot of times we'll receive requests from people that are outside of the state requesting contracts. With respect to parents, even if a parent is outside of the Commonwealth, we will still honor the request to access their student's records.

Also, representatives of newspapers and magazines, they must have general circulation within the Commonwealth of Virginia, and also radio and television stations and broadcasts. So the general process for filing a FOIA within LCPS is either email the lcpsfoia@lcps.org email address or submit your request through our website into the GovQA system. Even if that doesn't occur

and a person just says to a staff person at a school, "Hey, I'd really like to get these student records for my student," that should still be honored, and that staff person should reach out to either lcpsfoia@lcps.org, where the FOIA officer will input that information into GovQA. The reason why we use GovQA is it's our centralized platform for tracking so that we can communicate with the requester, provide the deadlines, and request an extension if needed.

So what are the timelines? So a public body has to respond within five working days. Working days mean days that the administration building is open. We count the first day as day zero. That's the day we receive the request. Day one starts the following day. And again, we do not count any holidays or days that the administration building is not open. If, for some reason, due to the volume of the request or the time it's going to take to gather the records, we may reach out to the requester and ask for an

extension. That's an additional seven working days. Common exemptions. If you've ever received records, you've probably seen blackout marks on the documents. We commonly invoke several exemptions. They will be personal records, so this will be information that's concerning another staff person or other employee of LCPS. Student records of other students.

If there is a dispute between two students, student A is a requester student, any information about student B will not be provided to student A in that request, in those responsive records. If information was subject to a closed meeting of the school board, that also will be withheld, along with proprietary information of contractors and attorney-client privilege or work product. I wanted to mention tests and examinations because sometimes this comes up.

There is a specific exemption for tests. Because they want to avoid someone learning the test, being able to share it with other people, or creating a disadvantage among other students.

As a general matter, LCPS does not charge parents for their students' records. Some divisions differ, but LCPS does not. However, if a parent asks for every substitute teacher that's ever subbed

at this school, that's a personnel record that's outside of the scope of their student's records. Our recommendations address both immediate program needs and long-term protections for special education services. We are recommending increasing special education instructional facilitators. Our SIS provide important supports to teachers, particularly new teachers and staff implementing specialized programs.

They help ensure that specialized instruction and interventions are implemented effectively and consistently across schools. We are also recommending additional assistive technology SIS to provide individualized technology, adaptive materials, and other specialized supports for students. We're advocating for the protection of special education teacher staffing, including secondary cross-categorical teachers.

Staffing should be based on students' needs, caseloads, required services, and program demands. Maintaining these adequate teaching staffing is essential to managing caseloads and ensuring students receive the services they need. We've identified the need to expand what's currently being coined the Tweener Program. These are students who remain on the general education curriculum and SOL

track, but many require significant adaptations, interventions, smaller instructional setting, or social emotional support to successfully access grade level content. These supports are currently inconsistent across schools, with a particular need at the elementary level and some additional need at the middle school level. We recommend prioritizing CAST transportation needs.

Students in CAST programs need safe, reliable, and accessible transportation. This includes replacing aging vehicles to ensure appropriate accessible transportation is available to those students. We are recommending adding adaptive PE staffing and scheduling. LCPS should have sufficient staffing and dedicated scheduling capacity so that

those students who require APE can consistently achieve those services. We are advocating for the development of additional public separate programming within LCPS. There is a gap in the current continuum for students whose needs cannot appropriately be met in their current school setting, but for whom private day placement may not be the best option.

An additional LCPS public separate option could provide the right environment and programming for these students. We recommend strengthening and appropriately compensating special education dean positions. These positions carry significant responsibilities related to special education programming, compliance, staff support, and school-level implementation.

We believe individuals in these roles should have appropriate special education knowledge and experience, and their compensation should reflect these responsibilities. We also recommend reviewing and clarifying the role and the reporting structure for this position. In addition to these immediate budget priorities, the executive and policy committee identified an important long-term concern.

As LCPS faces declining enrollment and possible future budget reductions, we believe special education should not automatically receive the same percentage reduction simply because overall enrollment has declined. A decline in total enrollment does not necessarily mean corresponding decline in the number of students requiring special education

services, the complexity of their needs, their IEP requirements, or the staffing necessary to serve them. For that reason, we are advocating for LCPS to establish a protected core of special education staffing and direct student services. Any future staffing or budget reductions should consider actual caseloads, student

needs, required services, specialized programming, related services, and special education obligations, not enrollment numbers alone. The goal is to begin this advocacy now before significant reductions are proposed, so that protections for students with disabilities are built into LCPS budget planning rather than addressed only after positions or services
